title: Norm Amplification, Psychological Safety and Academic Rigor
author: Lemov, Doug
summary: Lemov introduces 'Norm Amplification,' a classroom technique built on Peps McCrea's finding that behavior is shaped less by a teacher's approval than by a student's perception of what peers approve of. Rather than simply praising a good answer himself, Lemov argues a teacher's real job after a strong response is to surface the peer approval already quietly present in the room — nodding heads, students writing the answer down — so the responding student notices it. He walks through several concrete phrasings that convert an invisible social signal into a visible one. The technique is explicitly aimed at academic risk-taking: Lemov is careful to say the goal isn't generic belonging but psychological safety specifically for scholarly effort, so students associate visible intellectual risk-taking with peer respect rather than exposure. It's a compact, single-idea piece justified by a psychological principle and illustrated through one recurring example, a student named Kevin.
points: Peer approval outweighs teacher approval in shaping whether a student will speak up again — a cold-called answer's fate is decided more by classmates' faces than by teacher praise.
The teacher's move isn't more praise, but narrating the peer approval that's already present but easy to miss ('I see people nodding').
Getting other students to visibly write down a peer's answer functions as social proof, telling the original student their idea had value.
Asking 'how many people thought that too?' turns silent agreement into a moment the original speaker can see and feel.
The intended target is specifically academic courage — reserved for moments a student extends their thinking, not generic classroom positivity.
quotes: The idea that the individual's actions are shaped by his or her perception of what the group approves of is an observation we can use in the classroom.

But we should be aware that his mates (close knit group of peers) or his classmates (the wider circle of everyone in class) smirk or roll their eyes or look supremely uninterested & disapproving, the social norm is likely to win.

I might say: "Great. Thanks, Kevin. And I see people nodding their heads…" that last bit is the important part. It amplifies for him nascent signals he might have otherwise missed that his peers approved of and valued what he said.
That's Norm Amplification- my job is not so much to express my own approval but to help him see that when he is scholarly, his peers quietly think it's a good thing.
This has the effect of making Kevin feel like his thinking was shared by others, that he captured something they also were thinking.
The goal is to make students more confident showing their scholarly side and more comfortable sharing the full extent of their thinking.
